headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared project-directory workflows with broad egress and no default isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can exchange content through the project directory: agent_a writes files and has per-project shared state, while agent_b operates as an orchestrator with API calls and workflow metadata. That creates a plausible file-based injection path even without MCP or clipboard. The pathway is not proven by evidence, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF agent_b reads agent_a-authored files as instructions or prompts
IF both agents share the same project directory during a run
mitigations: Separate the agents into different project directories
Add a manual review step before agent_b consumes any file from agent_a
Prefix untrusted file content with explicit non-instruction markers
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from workspace files
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent file handoffs

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a has broad network egress and reads/writes the project directory; agent_b also has broad network egress and touches workflow metadata. If either agent processes sensitive files in the shared workspace, contents can leave the environment through model/API calls. The profiles do not show PHI or secrets by default, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared project directory
IF either agent sends workspace contents to its backend or external APIs
mitigations: Keep sensitive inputs out of the shared project directory
Use a redaction pass before either agent processes files
Restrict outbound network access during runs
Store only non-sensitive workflow metadata in agent_b
requires-engineering: enforce data-class filtering on all outbound requests

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, and its state is shared via the project directory. agent_b is an orchestration agent with API access and workflow metadata, so both can act on the same mutable workspace. There is no locking or coordination primitive shown, so overlapping writes can race and corrupt outputs; uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same project directory in one session
IF agent_b triggers actions based on files agent_a is still modifying
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate output directory
Serialize write access with a simple manual lock file
Run agent_a to completion before starting agent_b
Avoid concurrent edits to generated code
requires-engineering: add filesystem locking around shared workspace writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a writes generated code and can offer to run it, while agent_b is an orchestration/data-engineering agent that may consume workflow artifacts. If agent_b treats agent_a's outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade from code generation into downstream automation. The profiles do not prove automatic execution, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a-produced files as trusted inputs without verification
IF generated code or metadata is forwarded into downstream automation
mitigations: Require a human review of agent_a outputs before downstream use
Validate generated files against a schema or test suite
Do not let agent_b execute actions from unverified artifacts
Log provenance for every artifact passed between agents
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates between generation and orchestration

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles show no PHI, residency, or retention mismatch. The only concrete compliance concern is that agent_a handles an OPENAI_API_KEY while agent_b lists workflow metadata and broad egress, which is a limited secret-handling exposure rather than a documented regulatory breach. One-agent citation is insufficient here because the pairwise issue is weak.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in the shared project directory
IF workflow metadata includes regulated personal data
mitigations: Keep API keys in environment variables, not files
Exclude secrets from any shared workspace
Review retention settings for workflow metadata
Use separate credentials per agent
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning before file handoff
